title: A New Way of Working
audience: Advisory group, partner managers, frequent requesters
leaves: Partners know how to work with the team: how requests get an answer, when planning happens, what they will hear and when.

slides.html: Digital services at the DMV: how we'll work with you
slides.notes: Open conversationally. This is a conversation starter with our partners: what we see today, a different way of working together, and what it asks of you and of us.

slides.html:
Our current state of IT

Lots of work that takes a long time to get to

A big team full of committed individuals

A frustrated user base that can't get what they need to make their jobs easier

Big projects that don't succeed

A friction between the business and the technology teams
slides.notes: Only one line gets a check mark: a big team full of committed people. The people aren't the problem. Let the partners in the room nod; they live with the rest.

slides.html: How do we evolve to meet the needs of our community and our partners?
slides.notes: Pause here. This is the question the rest of the deck answers.

slides.html: We need to switch from a focus on output to a focus on outcome and impact
slides.notes: Output is what we ship. Outcome is what changes for people because of it. "We built what you asked for" becomes "we achieved the outcome you need."

slides.html: The client-vendor relationship most IT organizations use today
slides.notes: Walk the sketch. Client: "I have a problem and I can't handle it on my own. I'd like to save money and time." Vendor: "I need to listen, then figure out how, how long, how much." Then requirements, estimate, negotiation, order, delivery.

slides.html:
When client-vendor works

Works well

  1. "Fixed" output, like hardware
  2. A single client
  3. Clear requirements
  4. Only the client is affected

Doesn't work well

  1. Output that keeps changing
  2. Many clients
  3. Unknown requirements
  4. Client and users both affected
slides.notes: This is the fit question, and it's the honest center of the deck. Client-vendor isn't wrong; it fits fixed work with one client and clear requirements. Services that keep changing, serve many people and start with unknown needs need a different way of working.

slides.html: So how do we switch to an outcome focused way of working?
slides.notes: Use the pug. That face is the room's reaction: skeptical, fair, and the right starting place.
Digital services is a working model, not a team name or a technology. The next slides are its four tenets.

slides.html:
4 core tenets

of digital services

User-centric

Measurable impact

Empowered teams

Collaborative partners
slides.notes: Four tenets. The fourth is where partners come in, so spend a beat there.

slides.html:
User-centric

Putting the human being at the center of all work

Increase success

In a user-centric model, the risk of failure is reduced by constant validation against user needs.

Identify problems

Traditional client-vendor models can lead to a disconnect between what's built and what's actually useful to the end user.

Increase satisfaction

Focusing on the user experience increases customer satisfaction and long-term engagement.
slides.notes: For partners this means we'll ask to talk to the people who use the service, not only to the person who made the request.

slides.html:
Measurable impact

All work has measures attached, so we know if we succeeded

Results focused

Focusing on impact over output means we build things that truly add value.

Quickly pivot

Measures let us change course quickly by showing whether our efforts are making a real difference.

Measurable accountability

Data-driven insights improve stakeholder engagement, aligning expectations with real-world outcomes.
slides.notes: Each goal on the roadmap is a change in what people do, with a starting value and a target. Partners help us pick those measures and see them move.

slides.html:
Empowered teams

Teams guided by clear goals and accountable through measurable impact

Take responsibility

Team ownership of problems leads to more effective, tailored solutions.

True solutions

Space for exploration lets teams focus on solutions that matter, not just delivery.

Tradeoff decisions

Trusting teams to make decisions leads to better technical solutions and tradeoffs.
slides.notes: Partners bring the problem and the goal; the team works out how. That includes saying "a Microsoft Form solves this" when building software would be the wrong move.

slides.html:
Collaborative partners

Partnering on problems that span the real world and the digital one

Shared process

A shared problem-solving process bridges technical and non-technical work, aligning us toward broader goals.

Collaboration

Balancing ownership with collaboration is key when goals span tech and non-tech work and need investment from several groups.

One team

A shared belief in solving problems together builds one team focused on effective solutions.
slides.notes: This is the slide for this audience. The rest of the deck shows what partnering looks like in practice: your part in each step, how to bring us a request, and what you'll hear and when.

slides.html:
Traditional way of working

There is a problem

Come up with a solution

Ask the tech team to build to requirements

Tech team delivers software to fulfill requirements
slides.notes: This flow fits when the problem and the answer are both clear. Trouble starts when the solution is decided before anyone has looked closely at the problem.

slides.html:
New way of working

There is a problem

Partner with digital services

Set success measures and discover a solution

Test, iterate, release increments of value

Reach the goal that was set
slides.notes: The question changes from "what do you want built, by when?" to "what problem are you solving, and what does success look like?" Sometimes the answer is a Microsoft Form, and sometimes it's not building anything.

slides.html:
Example project:
VA website

UNITED STATES DIGITAL SERVICE

This works

Happening in the federal government
slides.notes: The VA story from the earlier version. Federal digital service teams changed significantly in 2025; check the example still holds before presenting, or swap in a state or regional one.

slides.html:
Not just the federal level, cities too!

Other cities: Philadelphia, Washington D.C., Chicago, Baltimore
slides.notes: City digital service teams. A local example would land better with your partners if you have one.
Now the practical part: who you'll work with, the steps, and your part in each.

slides.html:
Who you'll work with

Product manager

New

Owns the roadmap and the order of the work. The person to ask "what" and "why."

Product owner

Runs weekly request triage, owns the small request board, writes stories and accepts finished work.

UX designer and researcher

Elevated

Talks to the people who use the service and tests ideas with them before anything is built.

Development team

Builds in short, focused iterations, delivering value in increments so the problem actually gets solved.

Content strategist

Brings your requests to triage, leads training and guides, and supports champions.

You: partners and champions

Bring the problem, join the process, own the non-technical parts, and help your colleagues succeed.
slides.notes: Updated from the earlier version's four roles to the roles the system uses. The technical architect and scrum master also work with the team, mostly behind the scenes for partners. Steering and advisory groups come up on the "what you'll hear" slide.

slides.html:
The process

Eight steps in four stages. It runs as a loop, not a line.

Define

1. Capture ideas

2. Set direction

3. Plan the quarter

Discover

4. Discover: research, choose, test

Deliver

5. Slice the work

6. Build and release

7. Review the sprint

Enable

8. Enable: launch, train, measure, feed back
slides.notes: The earlier version showed Discover, Define, Design, Deliver and Enable, adapted from 18F. The system now uses eight steps; the four stages are only labels for grouping them. Discovery happens inside each piece of roadmap work, not once at the start.

slides.html:
The process

Define: steps 1 to 3

PRODUCT MANAGER (lead)

1. Capture ideas. Every request gets an answer within five business days.

2. Set direction. Each year, vision, strategy and up to three goals, with leadership.

3. Plan the quarter. A Now, Next, Later roadmap and commitments the team believes it can keep.

Your part: bring us problems, not only solutions. Join the advisory group if asked. The roadmap is open to you any time.
slides.notes: Replaces the earlier version's "Discover the current state" and "Define the future state" slides. The earlier version's lean canvas and roadmap screenshots are gone; the DMV roadmap, the filled example in the roadmap template, can go here.

slides.html:
The process

Discover: step 4

UX DESIGNER AND RESEARCHER (lead)

Research. Understand users and their "as is" process, your stakeholders, the landscape, the technology and the rules.

Choose. Name the real problem and line up at least three ways to solve it.

Test. Try the riskiest idea as cheaply as possible, then decide: build it, don't build it, or try something different.

Your part: connect us to the people who use the service, share what you know, and be open to "we shouldn't build this."
slides.notes: Combines the earlier version's "Discover the current state" research bullets with "Design the solution." "Don't build" is a successful result of discovery, not a failure.

slides.html:
The process

Deliver: steps 5 to 7

DEVELOPMENT TEAM (lead)

Build

Release

Review

Every two weeks

Regularly deliver small increments of value. Each slice works for someone on its own.

Learn early, make changes along the way.

Communicate often. A demo and a sprint report every two weeks.

Your part: come to the demos, tell us what you see, and say early if something doesn't fit how your staff work.
slides.notes: From "Deliver iteratively." The cumulative-outcome diagram from the earlier version is redrawn as build, release, review.

slides.html:
The process

Enable: step 8

CONTENT STRATEGIST and WHOLE TEAM

The people we work with stay part of the process and can keep going after the team moves on.

Every user can succeed with the service, not just reach it: guides, training, champions and support.

We measure the outcome and listen. Feedback goes back into triage and starts the loop again.

Your part: name a champion, release staff time for training, and tell us what isn't working.
slides.notes: From "Enable partners and users." Enable starts while the team is still building, not after launch.

slides.html:
How to work with us

Bringing us a request, and what you'll hear and when
slides.notes: New section, built from doc 08. This is the part partners will use most.

slides.html:
Every request gets an answer

Submit through the intake form or your content strategist. We review weekly and answer within five business days.

OutcomeWhat it meansWhat you'll hear
Already on the roadmapIt's already plannedA link so you can follow progress
Small requestA bounded change to something that exists, under one sprintWhen we expect to get to it, and when it's done
Large or strategicNew, bigger than a sprint, or could move a goalIt's in our idea log; we review it each quarter
Idea for improvementWould help people beyond youWe'll look closer when we plan next quarter
Will not doNot feasible, too costly, or off strategyNo, with the reason, and an alternative if there is one
Future considerationWorth keeping, but it doesn't fit nowNot yes, not no, and we won't follow up
slides.notes: Future consideration comes after the product manager reviews a large request or idea. It's there so nobody waits on a reply that isn't coming. A "no" with a reason builds more trust than silence. Bugs don't go through this review; they go straight to the team and urgent ones are fixed right away.

slides.html:
Bigger asks start with a conversation

Before a large request goes in the idea log, the product manager meets you to work through five questions.

1. What's the problem?

What happens today, who it affects, what goes wrong. Not yet the solution.

2. Is there a hard deadline?

A law, policy or funding date, or a wish? Mandates are treated as required work.

3. Do we need discovery?

If the problem is real but unclear, research comes before any decision.

4. Can the scope shrink?

A smaller version may solve most of it and fit as a small request now.

5. How do we work?

What can happen this quarter, what waits for planning, and when you'll hear.

You leave knowing

What happens next and when you'll hear from us.
slides.notes: Most large requests arrive as a solution with a deadline: "we need a portal by July." The problem underneath is usually smaller or different.

slides.html:
What you'll hear, and when

WhenWhat
Any timeThe roadmap is open: goals, what's in progress, what's next
WeeklyAn answer on every request submitted that week
Every 2 weeksA sprint demo you're invited to, and a sprint report on every commitment
MonthlyAdvisory group: partners and community voices check the work still fits
QuarterlyA new plan for the quarter and an updated roadmap
When it shipsRelease notes written for the people whose work changes
slides.notes: This replaces "communicate frequently (meetings and reports)" with the actual rhythm. Steering also meets monthly; partners usually hear its decisions through the roadmap and sprint reports.
